purpose: When does a partly filled container change the whole count required?
meaning: Floor chooses the greatest integer no larger than a real number; ceiling chooses the least integer no smaller. Dividing liquid volume v by container capacity c gives a dimensionless quotient x. Its floor counts completely full containers, and its ceiling is the least whole count with enough capacity for the entire batch.

definition.setting: A workshop must store v litres of liquid in identical containers that hold c litres each. Count the completely full containers with floor, then include one more container exactly when liquid remains.
definition.formal_latex: x=\frac vc,\quad f=\lfloor x\rfloor,\quad N=\lceil x\rceil,\quad r=v-fc,\quad u=Nc-v.

signature.c: Positive capacity of each container, in litres

conditions: Liquid volume is 0 to 30 litres and each container holds 1 to 6 litres. The model treats its entered real numbers as exact ideal measurements, with no tolerances or safety margin. At an exact integer quotient, floor and ceiling agree and no extra container is added. Otherwise floor is the greatest integer below the quotient and ceiling the least integer above it. General negative-number behavior is defined in the index but this storage scenario uses nonnegative quantities.
definition.domain_notes: The storage model uses volume 0–30 litres and capacity 1–6 litres. Entered decimal measurements are treated as exact. The whole counts use the unrounded quotient; printed fractional readings are approximate. The model has no measurement tolerance or safety margin. For negative reals the definitions still apply, but a negative storage volume is outside this scenario.

properties.derivation: By definition f≤x<f+1. Multiplying by positive c gives fc≤v<(f+1)c, so f full containers leave r=v−fc in [0,c). If r=0, f containers suffice and N=f. Otherwise f containers cannot hold the whole batch but f+1 can, so N=f+1. Thus N=⌈v/c⌉. At v=0, both floor and ceiling are zero.
